newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Grain-Gains seen on India, drought.
newsitem.headline: Australian Grain-Gains seen on India, drought.

text.p: India's surprisingly strong appetite for wheat and critically dry weather in southeast Australia have set the wheat market on a likely sustained upswing, traders and analysts say.
This is expected to be underpinned by another increase in the Australian Wheat Board's (AWB) pool price later on Monday.
"I'll call A$200.00 (a tonne) for the AWB pool," Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders said.

"I think they've been working toward that for a while and I think there's enough in the market to give them that," he said. In its last revision on April 1, AWB lifted pool prices for most grades by A$3.00 a tonne, taking benchmark Australian Standard White (ASW) to A$198.00.

Wheat, the best-performer among the range of Australian commodity exports in 1996/97, received a further boost on Friday when Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade Tim Fischer announced a one million tonne sale to India, 250,000 tonnes for July/August and 750,000 tonnes for November/December.

International circles had been speculating on the sale for weeks but non-committal comments by the AWB put the trade off the trail--- especially since India had already bought 1.3 million tonnes from Australia this year.

AWB general manager international Nigel Officer followed Fischer to say that India had not been expected in the market, certainly not for this large volume, but was re-building stocks. Fischer also announced Australia had sold 500,000 tonnes of wheat to Pakistan, but subsequent AWB information showed this was for April shipment and had been negotiated earlier.

The Indian deal sent Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) wheat futures up strongly on Friday in more distant contracts, solidifying virtual market-wide gains after price rises on dry weather concern earlier in the week.

Settlement prices for March, May and July 1988 contracts all rose by A$5.00 over the week. Apart from erratic September 1998, the only contract to lose value was near-term May 1977, which slipped by A$1.00 to A$180.50.

AWB wheat exports continued high during the week at 268,677 tonnes, steady with the week before. This brought exports so far this shipping year to 10.85 million tonnes, up from 7.53 million tonnes at the same time last year --- but attention was focused more on price prospects than on movement of this year's sales. Mitchell believes rising Australian prices are being primarily led from offshore as speculation runs high on unfavourable weather in the U.S. for both the winter crop, as it comes out of dormancy, and the spring crop.
Dry weather south of Sydney was also contributing to the rise and "getting quite desperate", he said.
"We're running out of time for rain to be beneficial in (southern) areas now. It'll soon be too cold, we won't get any growth out of it," he said.
Mitchell's belief that the market would continue to rise --- "we'll watch the U.S. market with bated breath now" ---was echoed by futures brokers.

Chris Gray of C.A & L Bell Commodities Corp Pty Ltd said on Friday that even though prices were already high, on balance the market appeared to have further upside over the next month or so after strong AWB sales and weather uncertainties in the U.S. "I think we'll see a very choppy but nevertheless upward

Over the past week Australian cash sorghum rose A$2.00-A$4.00 to A$137.00 a tonne farm Liverpool Plains. Cash new crop and old crop ASW both rose by about A$2.00 to A$140.00 and A$152.00 respectively. Cash barley rose about A$4.00 to A$135.00 on some shorts and lack of farmer selling.
